extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of early-18th-century periodical essays; general literate public and essayists
extracted.subtask_description: Composing short, moral or philosophical essays for a periodical (The Spectator-style), using anecdotes, classical allusions, aphorisms, and reasoned argument to instruct and entertain a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination before judging others
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you can be qualified to see and animadvert on the Failings of others, you must be pure your self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed via the Vision: the narrator is forbidden to open the chest of others' hearts until his own heart has been cut open, squeezed, and purified. Use moral examples or allegories that remind readers (and writers) to practice introspection and avoid hypocrisy when critiquing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character through vivid allegory and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: He examined hearts enclosed in transparent Phials, preserved in a Liquor; the 'Fomes' or Spot in the Middle of it signified particular vices (vanity, envy, passion, deceit, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete, memorable metaphors (e.g., spots, phials, liquids) to make inner moral qualities perceivable to readers. Demonstrate how inner vices manifest in outward behaviour by showing rather than merely stating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use named character sketches as exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vision gives many labelled examples (Tom Dread-Nought, Dick Gloomy, Will. Worthy, Freelove, Coquetilla, Melissa, Seraphina) whose hearts and 'Fomes' illustrate particular moral types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create short, recognizable character portraits with names and salient traits to embody abstract qualities (vanity, envy, prudery, deceit). These exemplars function as moral lessons and make philosophical points concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure philosophical argument with enumerated propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Having considered that Eternity which is past... I shall now draw up those several Articles on this Subject which are dictated to us by the Light of Reason, and which may be looked upon as the Creed of a Philosopher in this great Point. 'First,... Secondly,... Thirdly,... Fourthly,...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstract topics, present claims in a clear, ordered list ('First', 'Secondly', etc.) to make complex reasoning digestible. Use this scaffold to show logical progression from premises to conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine reasoned argument with theological/revelatory appeals when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay uses both natural reason ('Reason demonstrates to us that it has been') and Revelation ('Revelation confirms these natural Dictates of Reason') to argue for God's eternity and nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating metaphysical or religious themes, balance philosophical demonstration with references to revelation or accepted authorities to strengthen persuasion for a broad readership; acknowledge limits of human conception and adopt a modest tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support points with classical allusion and mythic anecdote
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and essays cite classical stories and authorities (Virgil, Dryden's Virgil, Æneas, Cybele, Hamadryads, Rhoecus) to illustrate reverence for trees and other subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical references, myth, and respected authors as illustrative evidence and ornamentation; such allusions lend authority, cultural resonance, and variety to descriptive or argumentative pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ concise maxims and aphorisms to distill truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The Love Casuist offers several Maxims in Love: e.g. 'There are more Calamities in the World arising from Love than from Hatred.' 'Love is the Daughter of Idleness, but the Mother of Disquietude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short, pithy maxims to convey general observations and to punctuate essays; aphorisms function as memorable takeaways and can summarize complex social truths compactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude abstract meditations with practical inferences and humble tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eternity piece concludes: 'I shall conclude this Speculation with one useful Inference... How can we sufficiently prostrate our selves and fall down before our Maker...' and counsels modesty in disquisitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After extended abstract discussion, draw out a usable moral or devotional inference for readers, and adopt modesty about the limits of human understanding. Turn speculation into an ethical or devotional application to leave the reader with a clear, affective response.
